utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-02-60-A, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May we take the appearances. First for Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I am told that no one heard the interpretation, so that I am not singular in that respect. Do -- do we expect some technician to attend?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the interpretation will now ensue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm told that after that brief hiccup we may proceed. Mr. Domazet, would you kindly repeat your appearance for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My name is Vladimir Domazet, newly appointed counsel for the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic since the 25th of February of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Domazet. And for Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Cynthia Sinatra, and Christopher Staker for Dragan Jokic. But I still have to complain. I have nothing coming out of my headset for the moment, no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, that's very serious, Ms. -- Ms. Sinatra. I can't. We'll have that remedied in a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you comfortable now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Milbert Shin, appearing for the Prosecution. And with me is with Mr. Norman Farrell, senior appeals counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then I should inquire if the parties can hear me in a language they can understand. Yes? The appellants? Mr. Blagojevic? THE APPELLANT BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I have been able to understand everything you've been saying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you able to hear, Mr. Jokic? THE APPELLANT JOKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I should say that Rule 65 bis, with which you are all familiar, requires that Status Conferences be held for each appellant in custody at intervals no greater than 120 days. This is the first Status Conference to be held in these appeals. It is being held within the 120-day period after the date each appellant has filed his Notice of Appeal; that is to say, the 23rd of January, 2005 in the case of Mr. Jokic and the 31st of May, 2005 in the case of Mr. Blagojevic. It was decided pursuant to the pre-appeal Judges decision of 14 April 2005 to schedule a joint Status Conference for the two appellants in order to facilitate the objective of synchronising and streamlining the two appeals. The date was then fixed for 23rd of June this year, but Ms. Sinatra, counsel for Mr. Jokic, had a difficulty in attending on that date, and so by a scheduling order of 6th of June, 2005 that date was then changed to today's date. I would thank counsel for Mr. Blagojevic and for the Prosecution for accommodating the change. Rule 65 bis, which has been referred to, is as follows. I would read it, though it is familiar to the parties. It is as follows: "The Appeals Chamber or an Appeals Chamber Judge shall convene a Status Conference within 120 days of the filing of a Notice of Appeal and thereafter one -- within 120 days after the last Status Conference to allow any person in custody pending appeal the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the mental and the physical condition of that person." Now, two purposes are to be served by a Status Conference: The first one is to allow the appellants to express concerns relating to, inter alia, the appeal and detention conditions; and the second one is for the Judge to update the appellants with respect to the status of their case. Now, each appellant - I turn to them - is invited to address the Chamber as to any particular concerns they have as to the detention conditions under which they are held or as to the appeal generally. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic has expressed to me that he has no complaints regarding his detention at the UN Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the time being there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Well, now, it is my turn to update the parties with respect to the status of the case. The judgement of the Trial Chamber in this case was delivered orally on 17 January 2005. A written judgement was filed on 24 January 2005. The case involves appeals by all three parties; that is to say, the two appellants there, plus the Prosecution. So there are really three appeals. The Prosecution filed its Notice of Appeal on 23 February 2005, and the Prosecution then followed that by filing its brief on appeal on 9th of May, 2005. Both Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic must therefore file their briefs in response to the Prosecution's appeal by 20 June; that is to say, by this coming Monday. Now, Mr. Jokic filed his Notice of Appeal on 23 February 2005 and his revised Notice of Appeal two days later, on 25 February 2005. Mr. Blagojevic filed his Notice of Appeal on 31 May 2005. Now, Mr. Jokic, having filed his Notice of Appeal on 23 February was later permitted by the Tribunal to file his appeal brief by 14th August 2005. Mr. Blagojevic, having filed his Notice of Appeal on 31 May, has until 14th August 2005 to file his appeal brief. The appeals of Mr. Jokic and Mr. Blagojevic are thus now on a synchronised schedule. They both have to file their appeal briefs by 14th of August, 2005. Further, in its response to the appellants' motions for extension of time, the Prosecution stated its intention to file a single brief responding to both appellants' briefs. Now, there are certain pending motions. On 6th June 2005, the Prosecution moved to amend its Notice of Appeal in certain respects that affect Mr. Blagojevic's case. No response has yet been filed. On 31 May 2005, Mr. Blagojevic filed a Rule 115 motion to present additional evidence. The Prosecutor filed a response to this motion on 10 June 2005. The reply is due today, 17 June 2005. The pleading process is thus still in progress, and it is accordingly too early to venture a prediction as to the further course of events. Are there any other matters which the parties would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing from the Prosecution at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Jokic has a few issues to raise with the Court today. If the Court will entertain our discussing a few administrative problems that we're dealing with, I'll address those. And then if you will allow Mr. Staker to address the Rule 68 discovery issues and disclosure issues that we must deal with immediately in order to follow some sort of deadline that the Court has set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to let the Court know that our brief, our response to the Prosecution's appeal brief, will be filed Monday, as -- as stated, and we have no problems with filing that. We also, as far as disclosure issues, we have -- I just cleared up with Mr. Farrell. We had a discussion just immediately prior to the Status Conference to clear up some disclosure issues that I was unsure of, but Mr. Farrell and I are working closely together at the moment so that no further motions regarding the May 2nd disclosure or any problems with the EDS, which we are just now acquiring by our team -- we should be able to communicate and search items with the EDS in the near future, but we have not been able to do so prior to this moment. Mr. Farrell has kindly offered us a hard copy of some of the documents that we require at this moment. We have a problem, though, in that most of the disclosure by the Prosecution, as far as documents go, are placed in our box, which is out in the security station here at the Tribunal. This is an appellant stage of the trial, and I'm not present in the Tribunal all of the time. Mr. Staker lives in London, and it was -- would be inefficient, I believe, for the Registry to pay for our coming back to retrieve documents. So we ask that the hard copies of documents, any statements, any originals that the Prosecution intends to disclose to us please be sent to me either in Texas -- I think that's the only solution, because otherwise -- this last time I didn't get the disclosure for two weeks because I've not been present in The Hague. So we -- they have given us some disclosure, but we just received a lot of it yesterday because we didn't have access to the box from our remote positions. I also would like to -- and, Your Honour, I know that if Mr. Farrell would like to respond to this and give us some suggestions on how to handle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear from Mr. Farrell. I gather that there's no question of willingness to make disclosure. The question is one of accessibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Just to clarify and, with respect, correct the present impression you may have. We have done only one disclosure in the box to Ms. Sinatra, and that was not two weeks ago. That was June 15th. And that was because we checked and found out that she was attending this Status Conference and thought it would be more efficient to give it to her when she arrived than to send it all the way to Texas. All other disclosures have been done through other means and we only did it because we knew she would be attending. I don't think there'll be any problem in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Sinatra?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am quite satisfied and I have no complaints and Mr. Farrell has been quite accommodating. Thank you. I also wish to inform Your Honour that we do wish to file an intended Notice of Appeal. I know the Rule says "with good cause," but this week, the day before yesterday, we just received a collection called the Drina Corps collection, which is maybe 600 pages to 1.000 pages of documents and CDs that we -- DVDs, which we have not had an opportunity to review. So I ask that Your Honour give us the discretion, once we've reviewed all of the new evidence, which we will be receiving all the way through September and probably -- probably past that date, that we have a right to file an amended Notice of Appeal as evidence is presented to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, let's hear from Mr. Farrell what his views are.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Just to -- just to clarify. It may not have been made clear to Ms. Sinatra, and we haven't spoken about this, so maybe I can just clarify for -- for the Court's sake and for -- for the sake of the Defence. The -- this week we wrote a letter to the Defence to inform them that the Prosecution was in the possession of a large collection. Ms. Sinatra is correct. It's a large collection. I think it's actually in the range of 300.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: 300.000, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And it is called the Drina Corps collection because it comes from the Drina Corps of the Army of the Republika Srpska. That collection, as we noted in our status report, is not available at the moment. It's presently being scanned in. I can explain the process, if you wish. But in any event, the period of time it will take, as it indicates in our status report, will be until the end of September till it's completely put on the Electronic Disclosure Suite and therefore made accessible so that all searches can be made for the -- by the Defence through the whole collection. And it's going to be all -- completely made accessible to the Defence. So in that respect the Defence may have -- have cause to review that collection in its entirety at the time it's fully made available. We're attempting to make it available sooner, and I'll of course inform the Defence of that and if the Court so requires, I can certainly notify Court. What Ms. Sinatra was referring to, in terms of the CDs that she received, is not the Drina Corps collection. She was informed of the pending disclosure of the Drina Corps collection. What she received in CDs was a disclosure of material related to evidence which came out of the Milosevic case which relates to events in Srebrenica. So as a result of the fact that there was evidence in another case related to events in Srebrenica, we thought it was obviously appropriate to ensure that the Defence in this case, as the events related to Srebrenica, were fully informed of that evidence and received copies of it. So I think that is the material that was recently received by the Defence. And the Drina Corps is a separate matter. But just to clarify, the material that Ms. Sinatra is speaking about is recent material out of the Milosevic case. That's the material that she's indicated they would like to review in time to determine whether or not they seek to amend their notice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra has announced her intention to amend her Notice of Appeal. Would you like to speak to that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, if I may reserve the -- the ability to comment on that until we determine what the scope of it is. If it relates to material that's just arisen, then we'll have to assess that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Farrell. I hope you do also, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. I do understand Mr. Farrell. I appreciate his ability to at least investigate and look at matters. And like I said, we have been working together well. I would like now -- Mr. Staker, as I had explained, is going to address some of the disclosure issues. If the Court will allow, I'll pass the -- the microphone to Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Staker, you have been all over the place, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I think that might be slightly overstating the case, Your Honour, but I have since moved on from The Hague. Indeed, my final appearance as a Prosecution counsel was, in fact, before you, Your Honour. It's an honour that my first appearance on the other side of the courtroom is also before you. Your Honour, before addressing the issue of disclosure, perhaps might I add an additional word relating to the proposed amendment to the Notice of Appeal. I would recall that towards the beginning of these proceedings the Defence for Dragan Jokic made a request that the Notice of Appeal deadline be extended until the judgement had become available in B/C/S. And Your Honour issued a decision on that on the 15th of February in which it was stated that that extension would not be granted but noted that after the judgement became available in B/C/S the Defence would be entitled to seek pursuant to Rule 108 to vary or specify in greater detail the grounds of appeal. Now, the translation, I believe, has only very recently become available, so with reference to that earlier decision, what I would propose as a matter of convenience would be simply that Your Honour give an oral order now that the Defence be simply entitled to amend -- to file an amended Notice of Appeal and that if the Prosecution has any objection to what is filed, the Prosecution can then file a motion at that stage to which the Defence would respond and a ruling would be given. The advantage of that procedure is that if the Prosecution has no objection, it will save the need for a formal written motion and a formal response and a formal written ruling of the Chamber. I leave it to the Prosecution to respond to that suggestion, but I think that would be of convenience to all parties, as well as to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, I need the benefit of your opinion on a little question. If there is to be an amendment of the Notice of Appeal, I -- I imagine that the decision has to be made by the Appeals Chamber acting in its full form or through the -- the Pre-appeal judge. Would you say that the Status Conference Judge has that competence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, I would hope not to have to take that question under advisement, Your Honour. My -- my view would be that there is no distinction in the capacity of a pre-appeal judge as a pre-appeal judge and a judge signature as a Status Conference Judge. I understand that it's one and the same capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you feel that the safe course would you for you to file a motion in the normal way?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Of course, if -- if that is the ruling, we'd only be too pleased to take that advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's hear -- maybe Mr. Farrell will agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I was about to propose, Your Honour, if there's no objection from the Prosecution, perhaps it would be not unsafe to proceed according to that proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Without seeing the content of the notice, I don't think it would be wise for the Prosecution to concede. Obviously the applicant will have to demonstrate that the grounds proposed were ones that only could arise upon a reading of the B/C/S version. And since both my learned colleagues speak English, I would presume that it would have to be something arising from the appellant himself. So other than that, I'm sorry, at this stage we can't consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I perfectly understand. Then, Mr. Staker, is it agreed that you would consider moving in the normal way?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: We would be pleased to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Having dealt with that point, I would then proceed to raise certain issues that the Defence has in relation to the proposed time frame for disclosure, which has been set out in the Prosecution's status report on disclosure. The particular concern relates to observations made in the status report relating to the Drina Corps collection. According to paragraph 6 of this status report, the material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have I -- have I got this status report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I understand it was filed, Your Honour. It has a cover sheet indicating a distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, I have it now. What paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It states that: The Drina Corps collection was provided to the Tribunal in mid-December 2004. It seems it then took a month to be delivered to The Hague and arrived in -- in mid-January 2005. And it is then stated further in the paragraph that at the moment it's anticipated that the bulk of the collection will be made available through the EDS by the end of September -- September 2005. Now, there are three particular concerns that arise from that last statement. The first concern is that it says that the anticipated time frame for disclosure is the time frame "at the moment," is the words used. And it appears that there's therefore no commitment by the Office of the Prosecutor to meet the proposed deadline by the end of September. And it would seem or perhaps the Prosecution can clarify that, but it would seem they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How do you work it out again?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, the second last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Says: "At the moment it's anticipated that the bulk of the collection will be available through the EDS by the end of September 2005."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: The words "at the moment" suggest that's the anticipated time frame at the moment but that it could change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, well, let's -- let's hear from Mr. Farrell. Do you have any thoughts on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if I could just respond briefly. The -- the time frame of the end of September, as we note in our status report, is at this moment the best information we have about when the EDS will -- will contain the Drina Corps collection. As we note also in our status report, we are seeking ways of having that -- having some portion of that collection available on the EDS sooner. This is something that's actively under consideration and we have exchanged some communication even today with the people who may be able to determine that. But at this point, our understanding is that the material will be completed being scanned in September and then will be available on the EDS by the end of September. But -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, is it -- if I understand you aright, these words "at the moment" do not signify any particular contingency on your side. You will have the material available by the end of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is my understanding of what the OTP is trying its best to do. I can't speak to unforeseen circumstances or difficulties relating to either resources or logistics that may arise. What I can say is that we will inform the parties and the Court of any variation or any problems that may arise in trying to meet that deadline so that all parties are informed of the progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, is -- is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this -- this was the first of several points I was going to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: To lead on to another conclusion. Yes. But I think what Mr. Shin has done is confirm what my understanding was; namely, that the Prosecution is not giving any commitment to meet any particular deadline. And that is, of course, the first concern. The second concern, arising out of the same paragraph, indeed the same sentence, is that it says that it's anticipated the bulk of the collection will be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Anticipated, that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That the bulk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bulk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: -- of the collection will be available by that anticipated date. So in addition to there being no commitment to meeting the end of September deadline, there's no commitment to, in fact, completing disclosure even by that date. It will be the bulk, but there's no suggestion as to any time frame for the disclosure of the remainder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: That is our second concern. The third concern is, of course, that the disclosure will be occurring - if the end of September deadline is met, which we understand now is not being committed to - some nine and a half months after the material came into the possession of the Prosecution. Now, we've been told the collection consists of some 300.000 pages. We appreciate that's a very large number of pages. But nonetheless a time frame of nine and a half months from receipt of the material raises very real concerns for two particular reasons: The first reason specific to this particular case is that the time frame that's been suggested, in our submission, must be expected to lead to delays in the scheduling of this appeal if the disclosure results in Rule 115 motions being filed. I do note that the final paragraph of the status report suggests that this time frame will not cause any such delay, but on our calculations it's difficult to see how that could be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Staker, if it becomes necessary for you to apply for an extension, wouldn't that be the proper course?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, that would be -- that would be one solution, Your Honour. But the difficulty is that the -- the accused has a right to a speedy trial, which applies also to a speedy appeal. In our submission, the disclosure rules can't be construed on the basis that the Prosecution completes disclosure when it's convenient to the Prosecution and that the accused must simply wait until then for matters to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, I think the Prosecution would agree with you on that, as I do. But is there any basis for saying or suggesting that the Prosecution would -- would allow this to stand over on its convenience?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting, Your Honour, that the Prosecution is deliberately delaying disclosure or dragging its feet. But I think in any national system, situations can certainly arise where the Prosecution believes that it's acting according to the best of its abilities but nonetheless there are legitimate reasons for the Defence to question whether the amount of time that things are taking is really appropriate or acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: And I would simply propose that the stated time frame is something that I think legitimately can be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Particularly in light of the three concerns I've raised. One -- one, the fact that there is no commitment to a specific date; secondly, that there's no indication that it will be more than the bulk of the material, with no indication of what will happen thereafter; and thirdly, the fact that the anticipated delay is some nine and a half months after the material has been received and that it will lead to delays, foreseeably, in the scheduling of this appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Farrell, are you in the position to state a time frame or to - or Mr. Shin - or to state -- or to state when you will have the entirety of the collection available?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if I could reiterate what I had explained earlier, that the information we have from the people who are dealing with the Drina Corps collection is that there is a firm intention to have it on the EDS by the end of September. But again, for the reasons I had alluded to earlier, it would be unwise or even reckless for me to undertake that this particular team on this particular appeal would have the ability to control the resources which are essentially at the hands of the entire OTP, including all the logistical problems that they face regarding documents from different sources, including translations. Now, if I could clarify a couple of points that Mr. Staker has raised, first, with regard to reference to the bulk of the collection. My understanding - and I'll give a very specific clarification of that - my understanding is the reason that it may be the bulk and it may be the entirety, but it may be the bulk because there are some 270 maps plus some hundreds of photographs. And those will be given a lower priority. And that is my understanding. They will be given a lower priority in the processing of these documents, including the stamping of the ERN number and the scanning of the document itself. And that's what we are referring to when we state "the bulk of the documents." The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You will make haste, of course?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We will undertake all efforts to -- to beg the people who are in charge of this process to make haste. This is a matter of priority for the -- for OTP resources. Certainly not only for -- because of this appeal but because of other trials that are pending in relation to Srebrenica and also other trials that involve Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There will be no -- no question of the Prosecution allowing this matter to drag on because of its convenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour. Absolutely not. One additional point I would add is that, as we note in our status report, we are making disclosures from this collection as material comes into our actual knowledge that -- that fall within our disclosure obligation under the Rules, and in fact that is how we have first informed the -- the Defence in this case of the Drina Corps collection because of a document that came out of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. Mr. Staker, the Prosecution has given their assurances that it is -- that it can conveniently give to you. There's no question of the Prosecution allowing the matter to be dictated by its convenience. If you find it necessary to apply for any appropriate extensions of time, well, then isn't -- isn't that a matter that you may consider in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated earlier, Your Honour, of course. Extensions of time is one way of addressing the problem. But it will, of course, always remain a matter of concern to the appellant that the process is taking longer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: A matter of concern to the Court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes. No, I appreciate what the Prosecution has said. I don't know if Your Honour might be minded to think that if a -- if a date were -- were fixed for completion of disclosure subject to -- subject to that being changed on good cause, that that might -- that might assist in focussing minds rather than leaving it on the basis that it be done as soon as practicably possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We have heard the Prosecution on this point. They wouldn't consider it wise to tie themselves down to a precisely stated time frame, and that, I think, counsel would understand, so that the remedy remains this: That if you judge it to be necessary, you will apply for any appropriate extensions of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. There were two additional small matters that I wanted to mention in relation to disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are you coming to an end any time soon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I do apologise if I am taking an undue amount of time for what is meant to be a brief Status Conference. I will try and make these two points briefly. The one matter rises in connection with paragraph 3 of the status report on disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Paragraph -- wait a minute. Let me get that. Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: It -- it states that: "The Prosecution is able to identify at this stage two categories of materials requiring review for disclosure purposes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: I simply wanted to clarify that the understanding remains that the Rule 68 disclosure obligations apply to the entirety of material in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor and not just to specific collections. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I would imagine that's normal, but let's hear from Mr. -- Mr. Shin or Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry that we're changing on you. It's completely normal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It's very normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate the Prosecution's clarification of that. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, Mr. Staker. You were once prosecuting counsel. The Prosecution isn't stating, as it were, a new position. It's affirming consistency with its standing obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I wasn't seeking to suggest the contrary by any means. No, no, no, I understand that is certainly a restatement of what has always been the position. The clarification that I was seeking was that paragraph 3 of the status report doesn't indicate any change in that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The final matter is that references are made to disclosure being made by documents being made available on the Electronic Disclosure Suite. I must admit the Rules appear to have -- the wording of Rule 68 has undergone some changes over time. My understanding is that the fact that documents are being made available on the Electronic Disclosure Suite does not detract from the provision of Rule 68(i), which requires the Prosecution to disclose material to the Defence which it knows to be exculpatory. I take that as meaning that paper hard copies will continue to be made available of the specific material which is considered by the Prosecution to be exculpatory under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear Mr. Farrell on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I -- once again, the Prosecution's obligation to disclose Rule 68 material remains unchanged. In relation -- if Mr. Staker is making a request to the Court that we disclose it in hard copy, then we'll see whether we can do that as a courtesy. But the Prosecution practice has been for a number of months that disclosure is placed on the Electronic Disclosure Suite in a case-specific file that is accessible to the Defence and they can access it then. Ms. Sinatra has brought to my attention a few difficulties, so of course we've tried to accommodate those requests. But the Prosecution's position is disclosure is being made through the EDS through case-specific files at the moment. If there's any problem with that, we can discuss it at a later date with Defence counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Staker?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I take it the Defence is -- is quite satisfied with that response. Sorry. I just wanted to confer with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: No. Unless Your Honour has anything further that I can assist with on those matters, I would lined to hand back to Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good of you, Mr. Staker. But I really don't have any other matter to mention at this time. Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a couple of more matters to bring to the Court's attention, if you will indulge me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yeah, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are also talking about a Rule 115 motion. I understand that Mr. Blagojevic has filed a motion requesting a hearing and the ability to present additional evidence. I would like the Court's indulgence on this matter because we have at the moment just returned from Bosnia and we do have material that fits -- we believe fits the criterion of Rule 115. It's being translated. But also, instead of filing a series of Rule 115 motions, if the Court would allow us the time to complete this review of this Drina Corps collection and then file one Rule 115 motion after this has been completed. I think it would be a more efficient use of the Court's time also and our resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Sinatra, wouldn't these elements be fit for incorporation in a motion by you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just bringing to the Court's attention that we can file a series of motions or we can wait until we've had complete disclosure by the Prosecution and file one motion at the end of the disclosure process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's see if Mr. Farrell is in a position to help on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection, of course, to the Defence taking the amount of time they need to put the material together. The only thing I would note is that we're assuming that the Drina Corps will bring about Rule 115 evidence, and maybe the better course of action is every certain period of time an assessment will have to be made by the Defence if they wish to file Rule 115 material. But generally, if the material is there and it doesn't affect the scheduling, then there isn't -- we don't have a general objection, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, there's no general objection by Mr. Farrell for that course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. Then I assume that we have the permission of the Court to file one motion at the end of the disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, file one motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And one more problem: We were talking about the EDS system. As I informed the Court, we have never had access to the EDS until hopefully in the next few days, but another problem with the EDS system is that it has incorporated Zylab and I think parts of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Zylab, which was a search engine that the Prosecutor had prior to this point and the Defence did not have. And also it should incorporate, I believe, the judicial database eventually. What's the problem with the EDS system for us - although we have not been educated on it quite get - is there is no indexing, there's no numbering, there's no way to -- to do a search that's efficient and effective at this time. That's why we still, even though the Prosecution has been informed that they should disclose materials to us in the EDS system in a file-specific compartment, we would prefer to have things disclosed to us at this moment on hard copy because of the search problems. Another problem with this is the judicial database is available to the Prosecution. The Defence has one computer terminal in the Defence room, and it's the only way we can search the judicial database is to be present here in The Hague. By August, supposedly, or September we would have remote access to the judicial database. So we're having disclosure problems and problems with access to tools and being able to utilise the tools provided by the Tribunal in the Defence counsel unit at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I must confess to you that I am all agog before the technicalities involved in your presentation. Maybe -- maybe the Prosecution can assist on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My technical skills are limited, Your Honour, but first of all we are required under Rule(ii) to disclose and make available in electronic form, so we are first of all complying with the Rule. Secondly, the fact that there's no index, no numbering, we get the collections and scan them in electronically into a large database and we have to do our own searches on them. So I don't know if I can be of much assistance, as we don't have any advantages of much difference. And as I understand that Ms. Sinatra is -- as of now Ms. Sinatra and Mr. Staker have now or will be receiving their password now. There is training available and there is actually a Defence working group on the issue of the EDS, so maybe the best course would for -- be for them to attempt to utilise it first and then we'll try to see if we can deal with some of the problems afterwards. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell has gone as far as he could go to meet you. There's no question about his willingness to comply with his disclosure obligations. And he's prepared to -- to meet you as far as the convenience to which you referred goes. But if you have any further difficulties, can you incorporate them in an appropriate motion to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask if the OTP might be willing to share their indexes with us, since they're scanning everything in and numbering it and indexing it in their own case. Perhaps we would be allowed to have the index that they're working from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter to which the Court can make any ruling. But we can inquire from Mr. Farrell for you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I am unclear of what indexes Ms. Sinatra is speaking of, so at this point -- I really apologise. If she'd like to raise it with me directly, I can certainly work on it. But I have no idea which index she's referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Don't you have -- I'm encouraged by the thought that you have been having conversations with Mr. Farrell. Why don't you pursue this in the course of conversations with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My only concern was that Rule 68, when it refers to electronic form - I don't have my glasses on - I think it's (ii). It was written before we had this EDS system and I think that the writers of this procedure envisioned CDs or floppy disk or something like that. This is just a massive understanding to find something, on the beach, a small pebble in the sand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But you accept that the Prosecution is in compliance with the provision as it is Presently worded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the Prosecution has every intent to comply as we move along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, then we -- we have all listened to Ms. Sinatra on those points. And I ask the Prosecution to take them in good faith and to advance the preparation of the case on both sides, on all sides, within a view -- with a view to an early hearing. Is there any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to state it's been a great pleasure to appear before you for the first time, and I look forward to working in this case with you, and thank you for your indulgence with our issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Ms. Sinatra. All right. Then we'll take the -- is there anything more? Then we'll take the adjournment at this point. Thank you very much. Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: There's no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try to be as brief as possible. I have not been able to take the floor so far. Perhaps French is a problem. If the interpreters prefer, I can also speak B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, no, it's fine in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No, the interpretation is coming through now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I support everything that has been said by Mr. Jokic's Defence counsel, but the Defence counsel of Mr. Blagojevic has encountered different problems. I would like to be as brief as possible. First of all, Mr. Blagojevic has been entitled to appoint a new counsel after the ruling rendered on the 17th of January, and I have noticed that since April 2003 he has not been in contact with his official lawyers. As I was a newly appointed Defence counsel, he did not want me to contact his former attorneys. The issue raised by Mr. Blagojevic's appeal is that I have been appointed on the 25th of February. On 23rd of March, 2005 I received from Mr. Karnavas something like 200 binders containing various evidence material. And thanks to your ruling, I was entitled to notify my -- Notice of Appeal before the 31st of May. But the difficulty this raises is the following: Since the 31st of May, you have granted those 75 days pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I have till the 14th of August to prepare my appeal brief. But in the meantime, I have also received the Prosecution's brief, and the deadline runs at the same time. I have 40 days in which to respond. My working language, as the Registry acknowledges, is French. I have never received the judgement in French, like Mr. Blagojevic, who received it on the 7th or 8th of June in 2005 in his language. There was no judgement available in French, and my knowledge of the English language probably suffices to read the judgement overall, but is probably not adequate to prepare myself for an appeal hearing. This is why I asked for an extension of time. These 40 days are 40 days which I need to respond to the appeals -- to the Prosecution's appeals brief or to prepare it afterwards, but unfortunately at this point in time in those 75 days, which expire on the 14th of August, I shall be working on my response to the Prosecution's appeals brief. I will have to file this this Monday, on the 20th. I honestly believe that as I am a newly appointed counsel in this case, where the transcripts amount to some 12.000 pages, if I were to do my job properly, which is what Mr. Blagojevic has asked me to do -- if I were to do my job and I'd like to do my job properly, I'd like to have more time. I would need more time to prepare my brief, which I need to file by the 14th or the 15th of August of this year. You also mentioned the fact that today is the date when the motion pursuant to Article 115 expires. This deadline expires on the 10th of June. I received this memo by fax, which was the day before I left home to be here in The Hague for this Status Conference. I left on the 14th, and I came to The Hague by car in order to carry some of these binders and evidence material which I have been given to work at home because I cannot review these 200 documents in the space of these few days that I'm spending in The Hague now. So I honestly could not file my response to the Prosecution's appeal brief, particularly as I had to file my response to the appeals brief of the Prosecution. As did Mrs. Sinatra, I received all the material today. That is another issue. All this material needs to be reviewed. But the most important issue, as far as Mr. Blagojevic is concerned, is that I have to prepare this brief by the 14th of August. This will not be possible. I would ask leave to extend this and extend it by 40 days so that I would have those 75 days. I would not include those 40 days which I needed to respond to the Prosecution. Another issue which was out of my control: I asked to have a legal assistant, Mrs. Lobagic [phoen], who is experienced in this Tribunal so that she could give me a helping hand. She was appointed and then was no longer appointed. I therefore had to look for another legal assistant, who was appointed towards the end of the month of May. So with all these difficulty I've had to come up against, I would like an extension of time in order to prepare my brief appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I listen to you with great care, but it does appear to me that the -- the two appeals on your side were placed on a synchronised basis and that basis would have to be carefully reviewed so as to get into a coherent pattern all the components of the litigation in question. What I would suggest to you is that if you feel that you need further time, could you please apply in the normal way so that the Appeals Chamber could consider the case on -- on the merits. If there are no other points, we will now take the adjournment. Thank you very much.
